events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Sgt. Pepper's Released
events.blurb: A four-person British pop group released an album that redefined popular music's ambitions. Recorded over 129 days, it experimented with orchestral arrangements, studio sound effects, Indian classical instruments, a pig from a farmyard, and a final 42-second tape loop designed to be audible to dogs. The cover showed the band as an imaginary marching band in front of a crowd of cardboard-cutout cultural heroes. It sat at number one on both sides of the Atlantic for months.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1967 (UK) — Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band by the Beatles. Peter Blake designed the cover; the cardboard figures included Marilyn Monroe, Karl Marx, and Edgar Allan Poe. Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr are the only surviving Beatles today.

events.title: Woodstock Festival
events.blurb: A three-day music festival, overcapacity within hours of opening, drew an estimated 400,000 young people to a dairy farm in upstate New York despite severe rain. Fences collapsed; the event became de facto free. 32 acts performed — Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, The Who, Santana, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Joan Baez. Two people died (one from an overdose, one crushed by a tractor); two babies were born. The festival became the defining symbol of the 1960s counterculture.
events.revealBlurb: August 15-18, 1969 — on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, NY. Hendrix closed at 9 AM Monday morning to a dwindling crowd with a distorted, feedback-laced "Star-Spangled Banner." The 1970 documentary won an Oscar.

events.title: Altamont Free Concert
events.blurb: A free Rolling Stones concert at a dusty California motor speedway, hastily organized as a West Coast Woodstock, instead became the counterculture's dark counterpart. Hells Angels motorcycle gang members had been hired to provide stage security in exchange for $500 worth of beer. Fights broke out throughout the day; during the Rolling Stones' set an Angel stabbed an 18-year-old audience member to death within a metre of the stage.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1969 — Altamont Speedway, California. The victim was Meredith Hunter, 18; the Angel who stabbed him, Alan Passaro, was acquitted on grounds of self-defense. The 1970 documentary "Gimme Shelter" captures the killing.

events.title: Rapper's Delight Released
events.blurb: Three rappers from the New York metro area, assembled by an independent label, released a 15-minute track over a bassline lifted from a recent disco hit. It was the first hip-hop single to reach the U.S. Billboard Top 40. The culture it came from had been thriving in parks and clubs around the Bronx for six years; this record introduced it to mainstream white America and set rap on the path from subcultural movement to dominant global genre.
events.revealBlurb: September 1979 — Sugarhill Gang on Sugar Hill Records. The bassline was from Chic's "Good Times"; Chic's Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards sued and received co-writing credit. The track went platinum in the US and hit #3 in the UK.

events.title: Spinning Jenny Invented
events.blurb: A Lancashire weaver, semi-literate and working out of his home, built a hand-cranked multi-spindle spinning frame that let one operator spin eight threads simultaneously rather than one. Later versions spun up to 120 spindles at once. Other weavers' wives in the district, seeing their cottage-industry spinning work disappearing, broke into his house and smashed his prototypes. He patented the invention six years later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1764 — James Hargreaves in Blackburn, England. Patented 1770. The name "Jenny" is probably derived from "gin," a contemporary term for a mechanical engine — not, contrary to popular story, after his daughter. Hargreaves died in poverty in 1778.

events.title: Great Reform Act
events.blurb: A long-delayed parliamentary reform bill received royal assent in Britain after two years of political crisis that nearly toppled the government. The act abolished 56 "rotten boroughs" — constituencies with almost no voters but a parliamentary seat still in the pocket of a local landowner — redistributed seats to industrial cities that had grown dramatically since the previous redistricting in 1429, and raised the adult male electorate from about 400,000 to 650,000.
events.revealBlurb: June 7, 1832 — royal assent by William IV, after the government threatened to flood the House of Lords with new peers to force passage. It was the first of a sequence of 19th-century reform acts; universal male suffrage in Britain was not achieved until 1918, and women over 30 the same year.

events.title: Suez Canal Opens
events.blurb: The French-designed 193-kilometre sea-level canal linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea — dug largely by corvée (unpaid forced) Egyptian labour over ten years with massive loss of life — opened to international traffic. A procession of 68 ships led by a French imperial yacht sailed from Port Said to the Red Sea over four days. The canal cut the sea route from London to Bombay by about 7,200 kilometres and shifted the geography of global trade.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1869 — designer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, commissioned by Khedive Ismail for the opening, arrived too late and premiered in 1871. The canal was nationalized by Egypt in 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis.

events.title: Bell Patents Telephone
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Scottish-born American inventor was granted a patent on "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically." Three days later he made the first recognized telephone call in his Boston laboratory, summoning his assistant from the next room. The patent, filed the same morning as a rival inventor's competing application, would become the most valuable patent ever issued by the US government.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1876 — Alexander Graham Bell. The first call: "Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you." The rival, Elisha Gray, filed his caveat a few hours later; legal battles continued for years. American Telephone & Telegraph, founded on Bell's patent, became the largest corporation in the world.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Peloponnesian War Begins
events.blurb: Tensions between a democratic maritime empire led by Athens and an aristocratic land-based league led by Sparta erupted into open war when Spartan forces invaded Athenian-allied territory. The war would last 27 years, consume Greek wealth, shatter Athenian power, and undermine Greek confidence in the democratic project. A historian who had commanded an Athenian force early in the war produced a narrative account considered a founding masterpiece of Western historiography.
events.revealBlurb: 431 BCE — Athens vs. Sparta. The historian was Thucydides. A plague in 430 BCE killed perhaps a quarter of the Athenian population, including the city's leader Pericles. Athens finally surrendered in 404 BCE after its fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami; Socrates was executed in Athens five years later.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: Destruction of the Second Temple
events.blurb: A Roman general's army of 70,000 legionaries, closing the siege of a rebellious Judean capital after a four-year Jewish revolt, breached the walls and burned the city's Second Temple on the anniversary of the first Temple's destruction 656 years earlier. The Temple was never rebuilt; a Western retaining wall remains the holiest site in Judaism. Roman troops hauled the Temple menorah and other sacred vessels to Rome, where a victory arch depicting the procession still stands.
events.revealBlurb: 70 CE — the siege was commanded by Titus, son of the emperor Vespasian. The Arch of Titus, completed c. 81 CE, still stands at the east end of the Roman Forum. The Western Wall is the most significant surviving fragment; Orthodox Jews mourn the Temple's destruction each year on Tisha B'Av.

events.title: Edict of Milan
events.blurb: Emperors Constantine and Licinius met in Mediolanum and issued a joint agreement granting every person in the empire freedom to worship any deity they chose — ending official persecution of Christians and ordering the return of all property confiscated from them. It was not technically an edict and did not make Christianity the state religion, but it permanently changed the empire's religious landscape.
events.revealBlurb: February 313 CE. The document was addressed to governors as a letter, not proclaimed as a formal edict — scholars still debate its exact legal form. Licinius, who co-signed it, was himself a pagan; Constantine had him killed ten years later.

events.title: Justinian's Reconquest of Italy
events.blurb: A Byzantine emperor launched an ambitious project to recover the western empire, sending a small but effective expeditionary force under his greatest general first to conquer the Vandal kingdom of North Africa (in 533) and then the Ostrogothic kingdom of Italy. The Italian war dragged on 20 years and devastated the peninsula; classical Roman civilization in Italy never recovered. The reconquered territories were largely lost within a generation to new barbarian invasions.
events.revealBlurb: 535-554 CE — Emperor Justinian I; general Belisarius (later Narses). The wars, combined with the Plague of Justinian beginning 541, depopulated Italy and ended the continuity of Roman urban life. Rome's population dropped from about a million in 400 CE to about 30,000 by 700.

events.title: Battle of Midway
events.blurb: Three aircraft carriers sank within six minutes after dive bombers caught enemy flight decks packed with fuelling planes and stacked ordnance. A fourth carrier went down the same afternoon, reversing a naval balance that had seemed permanent just weeks before.
events.revealBlurb: June 4–7, 1942. American code-breakers had cracked enough of the Japanese naval code to identify the target as "AF." They confirmed it by faking a radio message that Midway's water plant had broken — and listened as Japan relayed the bait verbatim. The US lost one carrier, Yorktown, which was sunk by a submarine two days after the main battle.

events.title: First Nuclear Chain Reaction
events.blurb: In a squash court beneath a university stadium, a team of physicists assembled 45,000 carefully machined blocks of graphite around pellets of uranium into a lattice the size of a house, withdrew a control rod, and achieved humanity's first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction — completing the key step toward a new category of weapon.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1942, under Stagg Field at the University of Chicago. Enrico Fermi's team celebrated with a bottle of Chianti in paper cups. The coded telegram sent to Washington read: "The Italian navigator has just landed in the New World." The reactor sat in a populated neighbourhood with no containment vessel.

events.title: Me 262's First All-Jet Flight
events.blurb: A swept-wing aircraft climbed away from a Bavarian airfield under pure jet power for the first time, reaching speeds that no piston-engined fighter could match, signalling that the era of propeller-driven military aviation was ending. The technology was real and available — but bureaucratic delays and a leadership obsession with bombers kept it from operational service for more than two years.
events.revealBlurb: July 18, 1942, Leipheim — pilot Fritz Wendel flew the Me 262 V3 on jet power alone for the first time. Hitler later insisted the aircraft be developed as a bomber rather than a fighter, reportedly costing Germany a 14-month delay. When it finally entered service in 1944, it was too little too late: fuel shortages kept most on the ground.

events.title: D-Day Landings
events.blurb: 156,000 Allied troops crossed the English Channel and landed on five code-named beaches along an 80-kilometre stretch of Normandy coast, supported by 11,000 aircraft sorties and 7,000 naval vessels. A massive deception operation convinced enemy commanders the real target was 300 kilometres further east.
events.revealBlurb: June 6, 1944 — Operation Overlord. Eisenhower carried a note in his pocket taking full blame if it failed. The "Mulberry" artificial harbours, towed across the Channel in pieces, unloaded two million tons of supplies in the months that followed. The first soldier ashore on Sword Beach was a British piper playing "Blue Bonnets Over the Border."

events.title: Battle of Anzio
events.blurb: 36,000 Allied troops landed almost unopposed on a beach 33 miles south of a major ancient capital, achieving complete surprise — then paused to consolidate rather than advancing, giving the enemy four days to rush in reinforcements and pin the beachhead into a cramped salient that became one of the bloodiest killing grounds of the Italian campaign.
events.revealBlurb: January 22 – June 4, 1944 — Operation Shingle. The initial landing met no resistance; soldiers reportedly bought wine and sat in cafes. Field Marshal Kesselring had the beachhead surrounded within a week. Allied forces took 34,000 American and 10,000 British casualties over four months before finally breaking out. Propaganda claimed "the largest self-supporting beachhead in history."

events.title: Epic of Gilgamesh Compiled
events.blurb: Mesopotamian scribes compiled the standard version of a long cuneiform poem about a semi-legendary king of a Sumerian city, his wild-man companion, and a flood survivor they visit in search of immortality. Earlier Sumerian poems about the hero had been circulating for centuries; a single scribe, working in Akkadian, produced the integrated twelve-tablet version that survives. It is the oldest recognized work of narrative literature.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1200 BCE — standard Babylonian version attributed to the scribe Sin-liqe-unninni. The poem's flood narrative preceded the one in Genesis by at least 500 years. Rediscovered in fragments in 19th-century excavations of Nineveh.

events.title: War and Peace Published
events.blurb: A 41-year-old Russian aristocrat completed the last serial installment of a vast historical novel following five aristocratic families through Russia's Napoleonic Wars. The finished work ran over 1,200 pages and combined personal drama, military history, and a 200-page essay on the philosophy of history tacked onto the end. The author rewrote the opening sentence at least seven times.
events.revealBlurb: 1869 — Leo Tolstoy. It was serialized in the journal Russky Vestnik between 1865 and 1869. Tolstoy later disowned most of his fiction on religious grounds and decades later attempted to destroy his own estate's copyright to prevent his heirs from profiting.

events.title: Ulysses Published
events.blurb: An English-language bookshop owner in Paris published a 730-page Irish novel by a 40-year-old expatriate author that had been serialized, banned, confiscated, and partially burned in the United States. The book followed a single day — June 16, 1904 — in the lives of two Dublin men, using stream-of-consciousness narration that shifted style dozens of times across its 18 chapters. The American mail service seized copies until 1934.
events.revealBlurb: February 2, 1922 — James Joyce, 40th birthday; published by Sylvia Beach at Shakespeare and Company, Paris. The setting day — known as "Bloomsday" — is celebrated by Joyceans every June 16 with readings, pub crawls, and costumed reenactments.

events.title: 1984 Published
events.blurb: A 46-year-old English novelist, suffering from advanced tuberculosis on a remote Scottish island, published a dystopian novel depicting a totalitarian state where history is continuously rewritten, all speech is monitored, and a figurehead leader is omnipresent. He had been working on it for four years; he typed much of it lying in bed. He died of the disease seven months later. The book gave English a vocabulary for surveillance authoritarianism that has never been matched.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1949 — George Orwell (Eric Blair). Written on the island of Jura. "Big Brother," "doublethink," "thought police," "Newspeak," and "Orwellian" all entered English usage. The title's year was chosen by reversing 1948, the year he completed the draft.

events.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Colombian journalist living in Mexico City published a novel tracing seven generations of the Buendía family in the imaginary Caribbean town of Macondo, blending precise historical detail with flying carpets, ghosts, and a character who slowly levitates. The first printing of 8,000 copies sold out in a week. The book invented "magical realism" as a recognized literary mode and cemented its author as the dominant figure in Latin American letters.
events.revealBlurb: June 5, 1967 — Gabriel García Márquez ("Gabo"). He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982. He wrote the book in eighteen months while his wife pawned their possessions to pay the grocer. It has sold over 50 million copies.

events.title: Google Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford PhD students filed articles of incorporation for a search-engine company they had been developing in a dormitory and a rented garage in suburban California. Their algorithm, unlike those of competitors, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them. They would never graduate. Their search index contained 60 million pages when they incorporated; it contains hundreds of billions today.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 1998 — Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The name is a misspelling of "googol," the mathematical term for 10^100. Their initial financial backer, Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." before the company formally existed.

events.title: Napster Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Northeastern University student released a peer-to-peer file-sharing program that let any user share their digitized music collection with any other user, anywhere in the world. Within 18 months, 80 million registered users were trading tens of millions of MP3 files a day. The recording industry sued; one rock band's lead drummer famously delivered a list of his fans using the service to Napster's offices in person.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1999 — Shawn Fanning. The suing drummer was Lars Ulrich of Metallica. Napster was shut down by a 2001 court ruling; the brand was later bought, sold, and reused several times, most recently by Algorand.

events.title: ILOVEYOU Virus
events.blurb: A 25 MB computer virus disguised as a love letter attachment from a known correspondent began spreading through Microsoft Outlook email clients at dawn local time in a Southeast Asian capital. Within ten hours it had infected over ten million Windows PCs worldwide, overwriting user documents, image files, and multimedia files with copies of itself. The authors could not be prosecuted because the Philippines at the time had no law against writing malicious software.
events.revealBlurb: May 4-5, 2000 — written by Onel de Guzman, a computer-science dropout in Manila. Damage estimates ranged from $5 billion to $10 billion. The Philippines passed its first cybercrime law in response. De Guzman was unmasked by a journalist 20 years later.

events.title: Snowden Leaks Begin
events.blurb: Two newspapers published articles based on documents leaked by a 29-year-old former NSA contractor, revealing that the U.S. government had been conducting bulk collection of American phone records from a major telecommunications company under a secret court order. The revelations continued for years; the leaker fled to Hong Kong and, after attempting to transit to Ecuador, spent years stranded in the transit zone of a Moscow airport.
events.revealBlurb: June 6, 2013 — Edward Snowden, via Glenn Greenwald at The Guardian and Barton Gellman at The Washington Post. Snowden received Russian citizenship in September 2022. Remains wanted on espionage charges in the U.S.

events.title: Cambridge Analytica Scandal
events.blurb: A former employee of a small British political consultancy went public with allegations that the firm had harvested personal data from some 87 million Facebook users, mostly without their knowledge or consent, and used it to build psychographic voter-targeting models for the 2016 U.S. presidential and UK Brexit campaigns. Facebook's stock lost $100 billion in market value in ten days. Its CEO was subsequently hauled before the U.S. Congress and the European Parliament.
events.revealBlurb: March 17, 2018 — whistleblower Christopher Wylie in The Observer and New York Times. Cambridge Analytica went bankrupt within two months. Facebook was later fined $5 billion by the U.S. FTC — the largest fine ever for a privacy violation, but about a month's profit for the company.

events.title: Tokyo Story Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 136-minute film about an elderly provincial couple who travel to the capital to visit their adult children, only to find them too busy with their own lives. Its stationary low-angle camera, dialogues shot face-on toward the audience, and refusal of conventional emotional climax embodied the director's signature style. Polls of international critics and filmmakers regularly rank it among the greatest films ever made.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1953 — Yasujirō Ozu. He developed the "tatami-level" camera position — 30 cm off the ground, corresponding to the height of a person seated on a tatami mat. It did not gain a Western reputation until the 1970s; Ozu had died in 1963, never having lived to see his international recognition.

events.title: Fellini's 8½ Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a semi-autobiographical film about a filmmaker suffering a creative block while preparing his next picture, in which the director's own memories, dreams, and erotic fantasies dissolve into the plot he is trying to construct. The Italian title referred literally to the number of films the director had made. It won two Oscars and became the classic film-about-film-making, endlessly quoted by later directors similarly stuck.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 1963 — Federico Fellini, with Marcello Mastroianni as his alter ego. Fellini had genuinely been blocked after a string of successes; the film emerged from trying to work out why. It was remade as a Broadway musical ("Nine") in 1982.

events.title: Apocalypse Now Released
events.blurb: An American director released a 153-minute film loosely adapting Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" to the context of the Vietnam War, shot over 238 days in the Philippines through a typhoon that destroyed much of the set, an on-set heart attack for his leading man, and a drug-fueled spiral for his support cast. He screened a rough cut at Cannes with the warning: "My film is not about Vietnam. My film is Vietnam."
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1979 — Francis Ford Coppola, starring Martin Sheen and Marlon Brando. The documentary "Hearts of Darkness" chronicles the production's mayhem. Brando arrived on set overweight and unprepared; Coppola had to shoot him in shadow from the shoulders up.

events.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial Released
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American director released a 115-minute family film about a stranded alien befriended by a suburban boy who helps him contact his home planet. The director had developed the story as a way of processing his parents' divorce and his imaginary childhood companion. The film topped the box office for 16 weeks, displaced Star Wars as the highest-grossing film of all time, and moved children to tears for decades.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1982 — Steven Spielberg. Composer John Williams won the Oscar for his score; Spielberg himself didn't. The flying-bicycle silhouette against the moon became the logo of Amblin Entertainment, his production company.

events.title: Jurassic Park Released
events.blurb: A 46-year-old director released an adaptation of a recent Michael Crichton novel about genetically resurrected dinosaurs on a tropical-island theme park. The film's digital dinosaurs — only a few minutes of CGI, mixed with extensive full-size animatronic puppets — changed the calculus of what visual effects could do. Audiences gasped at a Tyrannosaurus rex roaring over a rain-soaked jeep; a decade of purely physical-effects films were obsolete.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1993 — Steven Spielberg. The T. rex breaking into the jeep was actually animatronic; it malfunctioned often in the Hawaii humidity. The film displaced E.T. as highest-grossing ever. Spielberg was editing "Schindler's List" at night during production.

events.title: CNN Launches
events.blurb: A 24-hour cable news network began broadcasting from a converted country-club headquarters in a southeastern U.S. city, defying widespread industry skepticism that there was enough daily news to fill a full day of programming. The network's first broadcast began with its founder and his wife standing in front of an American flag. Its approach — continuous live coverage, rolling updates, no fixed broadcast schedule — eventually reshaped how all news was delivered.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1980 — Ted Turner's Cable News Network, Atlanta. The Gulf War coverage in 1991, broadcast live from Baghdad as bombs fell, established CNN's dominance. Turner had filmed a doomsday video, intended to play only at the literal end of the world, saying farewell to viewers.

events.title: Ghostbusters Released
events.blurb: A comedy directed by and starring several members of a Saturday Night Live cast followed a team of parapsychology PhDs turned paranormal exterminators in New York City. The film grossed $282 million on a $30 million budget and became the highest-grossing comedy to that point. Its theme song, written under deadline pressure, sat at number one on the Billboard Hot 100 for three weeks. A marshmallow man the size of a skyscraper became the film's most memorable villain.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1984 — Ivan Reitman directing Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, Harold Ramis, and Ernie Hudson. Theme song by Ray Parker Jr. The marshmallow costume, worn by actor William Atherton, weighed 45 kg and caused heat exhaustion.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from Aberdeen, Washington released their second album featuring a swimming infant reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. Within three months it had displaced a reigning pop star's record from the top of the Billboard 200, and its lead single's music video received more plays on music television than any previous video.

events.title: Spice Girls' "Wannabe"
events.blurb: A British pop group of five young women released their debut single — a bouncy three-minute track with a rap-like opening, shot on a single take in a Lisbon hotel — hit number one in 37 countries over the following months. The five — styled "Scary," "Sporty," "Baby," "Ginger," and "Posh" — would dominate late-1990s pop culture with a "Girl Power" message that was earnest, commercial, and enormously successful. They sold 100 million records globally.
events.revealBlurb: July 8, 1996 — Spice Girls: Melanie B (Scary), Melanie C (Sporty), Emma Bunton (Baby), Geri Halliwell (Ginger), Victoria Adams (Posh). The video was shot in a single day at the Hotel Palácio in Portugal. Victoria Beckham married David Beckham in 1999; she launched a fashion career later.

events.title: Book of Optics Written
events.blurb: While under house arrest in Cairo, a scholar wrote a seven-volume treatise on optics that correctly explained vision as the eye receiving light reflected from objects — overturning the ancient Greek idea that the eye emits visual rays outward. The work described the camera obscura, the physics of refraction and reflection, and the psychology of perception, and became foundational for later optical science.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1021 CE — Ibn al-Haytham was reportedly placed under house arrest after failing to deliver an ambitious Nile-regulation project he had proposed to the Caliph. He feigned madness to avoid execution, and used the period of confinement productively. The Book of Optics was translated into Latin around 1200 CE and was cited extensively by Kepler, Descartes, and Galileo.

events.title: Galileo Maps the Moon
events.blurb: An Italian natural philosopher directed a 20× magnification tube skyward and produced detailed drawings of the Moon's surface, revealing mountains and craters rather than a perfect celestial sphere as ancient philosophy held. He calculated the heights of lunar mountains by measuring the lengths of the shadows they cast.

events.title: Newton's Principia Published
events.blurb: A three-volume work laid out universal laws of motion and gravitation in mathematical form, explaining why apples fall and why planets orbit in ellipses with a single unified framework. The laws held that every mass in the universe attracts every other mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their distance.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1687 — Edmond Halley paid for the printing out of his own pocket after the Royal Society spent its book budget on a history of fishes. Newton later said a dispute over priority with Robert Hooke was the reason he almost withheld the whole thing.

events.title: Photoelectric Effect Explained
events.blurb: A paper explained why shining light on a metal surface ejects electrons only when the light exceeds a threshold frequency — never for very bright low-frequency light — by proposing that light itself travels in discrete energy packets rather than continuous waves. The finding resolved a long-standing paradox and extended the quantum idea from heat radiation to light, fundamentally changing the understanding of what light is.
events.revealBlurb: June 9, 1905 — this was the paper that explicitly won Einstein the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, not relativity. When the Nobel Committee finally awarded it (sixteen years late), they cited this discovery specifically. Einstein reportedly joked that the committee must have found relativity too controversial.

events.title: Gravitational Waves Detected
events.blurb: Two massive laser interferometers simultaneously detected a brief chirp of spacetime distortion that lasted a fraction of a second — the gravitational ripple produced by two black holes colliding 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal exactly matched the prediction of general relativity and confirmed that spacetime itself can vibrate, opening a new branch of observational astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: Detected September 14, 2015; announced February 11, 2016 — the team waited five months to check for errors. The signal lasted 0.2 seconds. One scientist described hearing the chirp played as audio as "nature singing to us." Three founders of LIGO — Weiss, Barish, and Thorne — shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.

events.title: Susan B. Anthony Votes
events.blurb: A 52-year-old suffragist and 14 other women presented themselves at a polling place in their upstate New York city and demanded to register to vote, citing the language of the recently ratified 14th Amendment. Three inspectors, after consulting the U.S. constitution, let them register. On election day four days later she voted; she was arrested two weeks after that. Her trial, the following year, denied her the right to testify in her own defense.
events.revealBlurb: November 5, 1872 — Rochester, NY. Judge Ward Hunt fined her $100; she refused ever to pay. The U.S. has since put her face on a coin that was widely disliked and quickly withdrawn (the 1979 dollar).

events.title: Amelia Earhart Disappears
events.blurb: On the penultimate leg of an around-the-world flight at the equator, a 39-year-old American aviator and her navigator took off from a Pacific airstrip bound for a tiny coral island 4,100 kilometres away. Her final radio messages reported low fuel and inability to locate the island. A Navy search of 400,000 square kilometres of ocean found nothing. Her disappearance has launched a hundred books and at least three feature films.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1937 — Earhart and Fred Noonan bound for Howland Island. Prevailing theories: ran out of fuel and ditched; landed on uninhabited Nikumaroro and died of thirst; captured by the Japanese. No conclusive physical evidence exists.

events.title: Equal Pay Act Signed
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed legislation making it unlawful for employers to pay women less than men for equal work on jobs requiring equal skill, effort, and responsibility. The law had been introduced 18 years earlier and passed only after being narrowed so far that it exempted executive, administrative, and professional employees — and explicitly did not cover many of the sex-segregated job categories where the pay gap was worst.
events.revealBlurb: June 10, 1963 — John F. Kennedy. It amended the Fair Labor Standards Act. The wage gap between full-time working men and women has narrowed from 60 cents on the dollar in 1963 to roughly 82 cents today — not yet zero, and progress stalled for most of the 2010s.

events.title: Valentina Tereshkova in Space
events.blurb: A 26-year-old textile-factory worker and amateur parachutist from a provincial Russian town orbited Earth 48 times over nearly three days aboard a Vostok capsule, becoming the first woman in space. She was two decades ahead of the next woman cosmonaut. Western intelligence had no idea the Soviet Union had even trained female cosmonauts. The mission, like all Soviet space missions, was announced only after the launch.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1963 — Vostok 6. Her call sign was "Chaika" (Seagull). Over half a century later, aged 85, Tereshkova remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission. The next Soviet woman cosmonaut flew 19 years later.

events.title: Margaret Thatcher Becomes PM
events.blurb: The leader of the British Conservative Party, a grocer's daughter who had studied chemistry at Oxford and later trained as a barrister, was invited by the monarch to form a government after her party won a sweeping parliamentary majority. She became the United Kingdom's first woman prime minister and would hold the office for 11 years — the longest continuous premiership of the 20th century.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1979 — she took office quoting St. Francis of Assisi on the doorstep: "Where there is discord, may we bring harmony." The next decade would be anything but that. She was forced to resign by her own cabinet in November 1990.

events.title: Death of Alexander the Great
events.blurb: A Macedonian king who had conquered territory from Greece to northwest India died after a two-week fever in Nebuchadnezzar's palace in Babylon, aged 32. His generals immediately divided his empire into competing successor kingdoms, triggering a half-century of wars called the Wars of the Diadochi.

events.title: First Punic War Begins
events.blurb: The Roman Republic and the Carthaginian Empire, the two rising powers of the western Mediterranean, went to war over control of a large island between them. The conflict would last 23 years and transform Rome from a purely land-based power into a naval one — the Romans, ignorant of shipbuilding, reportedly reverse-engineered a captured Carthaginian warship to build their first fleet. Rome eventually won and imposed a crushing indemnity; the seed of two more wars was planted.
events.revealBlurb: 264 BCE — Rome vs. Carthage over Sicily. "Punic" comes from the Latin for "Phoenician," Carthage's origin. The Romans invented boarding bridges ("corvi") that turned sea battles into quasi-land battles they could win. Rome lost 700 ships over the course of the war, mostly to storms.

events.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.blurb: A group of Roman senators led by Cassius and Brutus surrounded the dictator in the Theatre of Pompey and stabbed him twenty-three times. A later physician concluded only one wound was fatal; the man fell at the base of a statue of his former rival, Pompey himself.
events.revealBlurb: The Ides of March, 44 BCE. Caesar had been warned by a soothsayer to "beware the Ides of March" and laughed it off the same morning. His last words, "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare — ancient sources quote him saying "You too, child?" in Greek.

events.title: Hadrian's Wall Begun
events.blurb: A Roman emperor, touring his empire's northern frontier in Britannia, ordered the construction of a 117-kilometre stone-and-turf fortification across the narrow neck of the island from coast to coast. Sixteen forts and dozens of smaller milecastles were strung along it, garrisoned by auxiliary troops from across the empire. It was less a continuous fighting wall than a filter — controlling movement, collecting customs, and projecting imperial authority. Much of it still stands; the wall defined the political frontier for three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 122 CE — Emperor Hadrian. Construction took six years and employed three legions. Hadrian himself famously declared at the start of his reign that Rome would not continue to expand its borders indefinitely — reversing his predecessor Trajan's conquests in Mesopotamia.

events.title: Battle of Adrianople
events.blurb: After Rome settled Visigothic refugees south of the Danube and then systematically starved and abused them, the Goths rose in revolt. Emperor Valens — who refused to wait for reinforcements — attacked their fortified camp with approximately 30,000 men. Gothic cavalry flanked both sides of the Roman line and trapped the legions; two-thirds of the eastern field army was destroyed and Valens himself was killed.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 378 CE. Valens's body was never found. One account says he was carried wounded to a farmhouse, which Gothic soldiers then set alight; another says he was lost in the general slaughter. Military historians sometimes call Adrianople "the ancient world's Stalingrad."

events.title: 14th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Ratified in the aftermath of civil war, a constitutional amendment granted citizenship to "all persons born or naturalized in the United States," promised them equal protection under the laws, and guaranteed due process. Its sweeping language became, a century later, the foundation of Supreme Court rulings on school segregation, interracial marriage, abortion, and marriage equality.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1868 — citizenship via birthright. Its authors were thinking of formerly enslaved people; its practical effect reshaped virtually every area of American law. The "equal protection clause" alone has been cited in over 400 Supreme Court cases.

events.title: Medgar Evers Assassinated
events.blurb: The NAACP's field secretary in a Southern state was shot in the back in his own driveway as he returned home at 12:30 AM from a meeting, carrying T-shirts that read "Jim Crow Must Go." He died in front of his wife and three children. His killer, a Ku Klux Klan member, was tried twice; both trials ended in hung juries with all-white panels. He walked free for 31 years.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1963 — Jackson, Mississippi. His killer, Byron De La Beckwith, was finally convicted in 1994 after new witnesses came forward. Medgar's widow Myrlie Evers-Williams spent decades pursuing the case; she later chaired the NAACP.

events.title: Loving v. Virginia
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously struck down the laws of sixteen states prohibiting interracial marriage, after a Virginia couple — a white construction worker and his Black and Native American wife — had been awakened in their bed, arrested, and sentenced to a year in jail for being married. The Court called the bans "measures designed to maintain White Supremacy."
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1967 — Richard and Mildred Loving. They had been legally married in Washington D.C. and returned home to Virginia. Their surname's poetic appropriateness is real, not invented. June 12 is now informally "Loving Day."

events.title: Thurgood Marshall Confirmed
events.blurb: The U.S. Senate confirmed the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court by a vote of 69-11 after a contentious hearing in which Southern senators grilled him on obscure constitutional questions in an effort to embarrass him. He had already argued 32 cases before the Court — and won 29 — as the NAACP's lead attorney. He served 24 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 30, 1967 — confirmed to replace Tom Clark. Lyndon Johnson had said bluntly on tape: "I want folks to look up and see a Negro lawyer up there." Marshall was the grandson of a slave and had been rejected by the University of Maryland law school on racial grounds.

events.title: Barack Obama Elected President
events.blurb: A first-term U.S. senator, 47 years old and the son of a Kenyan father and Kansan mother, defeated his Republican opponent by a nine-million-vote margin to become the 44th President of the United States and the first Black person elected to the office. He carried states no Democrat had won in decades, including Indiana and North Carolina.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 2008 — defeating John McCain. Obama gave his victory speech in Chicago's Grant Park before 200,000 people. Jesse Jackson, standing in the crowd, wept on camera. Michelle Obama became the first African-American First Lady.

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.

events.title: Atomic Bomb Dropped on Hiroshima
events.blurb: At 8:15 that morning, a B-29 Superfortress named the Enola Gay released a uranium bomb nicknamed "Little Boy" over the Japanese city of Hiroshima, which detonated at 1,968 feet above the city center with a force equivalent to approximately 15,000 tons of TNT. Estimates of deaths in the four months following the explosion range from 90,000 to 166,000; roughly two-thirds of the city's buildings were destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — Hiroshima, Japan. "Little Boy" was the first nuclear weapon ever used in warfare, but it had never been fully tested — scientists were confident enough in the gun-type design. Japan did not surrender after Hiroshima; it took a second bomb (Nagasaki, August 9) to produce the surrender announcement.

events.title: Apollo 1 Launchpad Fire
events.blurb: During a ground test at Cape Kennedy that afternoon, a fire broke out inside the Apollo 1 command module, killing all three crew members — Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee — in less than a minute. The cause was an electrical spark in an atmosphere of pure oxygen at elevated pressure, and the hatch could not be opened quickly enough to save anyone.
events.revealBlurb: January 27, 1967 — Launch Complex 34, Cape Kennedy, Florida. The crew could not escape because the hatch required 90 seconds to open inward — and the fire created pressure that made it impossible to swing. The disaster set the Moon program back 20 months but ultimately produced a safer spacecraft.

events.title: Watergate Break-In
events.blurb: At 2:30 in the morning, Washington D.C. police arrested five men inside the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate complex, where they had broken in to photograph documents and plant surveillance devices. The burglars were connected to the Committee to Re-Elect the President, and the discovery of the break-in and the subsequent cover-up by the Nixon White House eventually destroyed his presidency.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1972 — Watergate complex, Washington, D.C. The burglars were caught because a security guard noticed tape on a door latch and called the police. Nixon won re-election in November 1972 in one of the largest landslides in American history — 520 to 17 electoral votes — while the cover-up was already underway.

events.title: Reagan: "Tear Down This Wall"
events.blurb: Standing 100 yards from the concrete barrier dividing East and West Berlin that afternoon, President Ronald Reagan delivered a speech at the Brandenburg Gate in which he directly challenged Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev: "Mr. Gorbachev, tear down this wall!" His own State Department and National Security Council had urged him to remove the line as counterproductively provocative; Reagan insisted on keeping it.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1987 — Brandenburg Gate, West Berlin. At the time, the speech received relatively little media coverage and was dismissed as Cold War posturing by Soviet state media. Two years, four months, and 27 days later, the wall fell.

events.title: First World Series
events.blurb: A best-of-nine championship series between the American League and National League pennant winners was played — the first time the two major leagues had agreed to a postseason championship after years of cold war. An underdog American League team, the Boston Americans, defeated the heavily favoured Pittsburgh Pirates 5 games to 3. The Pirates' owner, Barney Dreyfuss, had proposed the series himself.
events.revealBlurb: October 1-13, 1903 — Boston Americans (later the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates. Cy Young, Boston's 36-year-old ace, started game 3 but was the losing pitcher. Dreyfuss gave his losing Pirates a share of the winners' purse to compensate. No World Series was held in 1904; it became annual from 1905.

events.title: Ali vs. Frazier I
events.blurb: The first meeting between two undefeated heavyweight boxing champions — one reigning, one returning from a 43-month ring absence after losing his license for refusing the Vietnam War draft — was held at a New York arena before a celebrity-packed crowd. The fight went the full 15 rounds; the defending champion landed a left hook in the 15th that put the challenger on the canvas and won a unanimous decision. It was billed as the Fight of the Century and delivered.
events.revealBlurb: March 8, 1971 — Joe Frazier defeated Muhammad Ali at Madison Square Garden. Both fighters were paid $2.5 million — unprecedented for any boxing match. Frank Sinatra shot ringside photos for Life magazine. Ali would win their 1974 rematch and the 1975 "Thrilla in Manila" decider.

events.title: Secretariat Wins the Triple Crown
events.blurb: A three-year-old chestnut colt won the Belmont Stakes by 31 lengths in a world-record time of 2 minutes 24 seconds, becoming the first Triple Crown winner in 25 years. His margin of victory and track record remain unmatched; television viewers watching the broadcast described the race as looking like a different event from the others.

events.title: Michael Jordan's Last Shot
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Chicago Bulls star took a jump shot from the top of the key with 5.2 seconds remaining in game 6 of an NBA Finals, giving his team an 87-86 lead over the Utah Jazz in a Salt Lake City arena. Jordan's defender had slipped; the shot rattled home. The Jazz could not tie; the Bulls clinched their sixth championship in eight years. It was the last shot Jordan would take as a Chicago Bull; within weeks the team would break up and he would retire for the second time.
events.revealBlurb: June 14, 1998 — Michael Jordan's "Last Shot" over Bryon Russell. He scored the Bulls' final 8 points of the game. The 1997-98 team was documented in ESPN's 2020 "The Last Dance," which drew enormous audiences during the COVID pandemic lockdown.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Sack of Lindisfarne
events.blurb: A band of Scandinavian raiders beached their longships on the tidal island home of an isolated monastery off the northeast coast of England, slaughtered the monks, and plundered the gold and silver from the gilded shrines. The attack shocked Christian Europe, which had not imagined its remote religious outposts were vulnerable. It marks the conventional beginning of the Viking Age.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 793 — the monks had left their community undefended on the assumption that the sea was a barrier rather than a road. Alcuin, one of Charlemagne's advisers, wrote: "Never before has such terror appeared in Britain as we have suffered from this pagan race."

events.title: William the Conqueror Crowned
events.blurb: Ten weeks after winning a decisive battle on the south coast of England, the Norman duke who had invaded was crowned king at a Westminster abbey. During the coronation, Norman guards outside the abbey mistook acclamations for riot and set fire to nearby houses; the new king was hurriedly anointed while smoke drifted through the doors. He would never be popular with his new subjects.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1066 — Westminster Abbey. William spent the next two decades building castles, compiling the Domesday Book, and crushing rebellions. He was buried in Caen, and his tomb was opened, profaned, and emptied of bones during the French Revolution.

events.title: Magna Carta Sealed
events.blurb: Facing armed revolt by his barons after a series of disastrous foreign wars and arbitrary taxation, an English king met them in a meadow beside the Thames and affixed his seal to a 63-clause charter limiting royal power, guaranteeing trial by peers, and making free men subject only to "the law of the land." He repudiated it within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
events.revealBlurb: June 15, 1215 — King John at Runnymede. Only three original copies survive. Clauses against arbitrary imprisonment echo today through American due-process law. The barons were self-interested, not democratic, but the language was universal enough to outlive them.

events.title: Fall of Granada
events.blurb: The last Muslim ruler of an Andalusian emirate, besieged for seven months in his Alhambra palace, handed over its keys to Castilian and Aragonese monarchs and rode into exile, reportedly sighing at his final view from a mountain pass. The surrender ended 781 years of Muslim political presence on the Iberian peninsula. The same monarchs, three months later, would commission an Italian sailor to seek a western route to Asia.
events.revealBlurb: January 2, 1492 — Ferdinand and Isabella accept the surrender of Muhammad XII (Boabdil). His mother is said to have told him: "You weep like a woman for what you could not defend like a man." Columbus was at the Alhambra that summer presenting his proposal.

events.title: First Woman in Space
events.blurb: Valentina Tereshkova, a 26-year-old former textile factory worker and amateur parachutist with no pilot training, launched aboard Vostok 6 and orbited Earth 48 times over nearly three days — more total time in space than all US astronauts who had flown to that date combined. She performed observations and photographed aerosol layers in Earth's atmosphere before parachuting to a landing in Kazakhstan.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1963 — Vostok 6. Tereshkova selected herself from 400 applicants by writing a letter directly to the Soviet Space Program. She reportedly got motion sick and did not conduct some planned manual maneuvers, a fact kept classified for years. No woman flew in space again for 19 years. She remains the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

events.title: Lunar Surface Landing
events.blurb: A spacecraft descended onto the Sea of Tranquility with 25 seconds of fuel remaining after the landing computer triggered five 1202 alarms caused by executive overflow. Two crew members spent 2 hours 31 minutes on the surface, collecting 21.5 kg of rock and soil and deploying a seismometer and a retroreflector array.
events.revealBlurb: July 20, 1969 — Apollo 11. Armstrong's first step came at 10:56 PM Eastern. The descent stage still sits on the Moon; the flag was knocked flat by the liftoff exhaust. The line was supposed to be "one small step for a man" — the transmission dropped the article, and Armstrong spent decades insisting he said it.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: Water Confirmed on the Moon
events.blurb: India's Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe detected spectral signatures consistent with water molecules during its 25-minute controlled descent to the lunar south pole, with readings from a mass spectrometer increasing steadily as the probe flew toward higher latitudes. Three instruments on the orbiting spacecraft corroborated the finding, confirming that water ice is present across the lunar surface.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 2008 — Chandrayaan-1/MIP. The probe was decorated with the Indian national flag and crashed intentionally near Shackleton Crater at 85° south — making India the fourth nation to place an object on the Moon. The water discovery reversed decades of scientific consensus that the Moon was bone dry, reshaping plans for every future lunar base concept.

events.title: First Commercial Crewed Orbital Launch
events.blurb: SpaceX Crew Dragon Endeavour launched two NASA astronauts to the International Space Station, marking the first crewed orbital launch from American soil since the Space Shuttle's retirement nine years earlier and the first time a commercially built and operated vehicle carried NASA astronauts to orbit. The spacecraft docked with the ISS approximately 19 hours after liftoff.
events.revealBlurb: May 30, 2020 — Demo-2. The launch was originally scrubbed three days earlier at T-17 minutes due to a storm. Astronaut Doug Hurley — who had piloted the final Shuttle mission in 2011 — flew his second "last American launch from US soil" in nine years, except this time it wasn't the last. The touchscreen controls in the Dragon capsule replaced 800+ switches.

events.title: Great Wall of China Begun
events.blurb: The first emperor of a unified Chinese state, having conquered the six rival warring kingdoms, ordered existing regional defensive walls in the north linked into a continuous frontier fortification against nomadic incursions. A conscripted army of 300,000 labourers worked for years; many died on the project and were, according to tradition, buried in its foundations. The Ming-dynasty wall, which is what most modern visitors see, was rebuilt over a millennium later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 220 BCE — Qin Shi Huang. The visible stone-and-brick wall is largely Ming-dynasty (1368-1644), built with much better materials. The Qin wall was mostly earthen and only fragments survive. Total length, across all versions, has been measured at 21,196 km.

events.title: Colosseum Inaugurated
events.blurb: A Roman emperor inaugurated a 50,000-capacity elliptical amphitheatre in the capital with 100 consecutive days of gladiatorial games, executions, and staged hunts that killed 9,000 animals. The structure was four stories tall, constructed in travertine and concrete, with a retractable canvas awning (velarium) to shade the spectators. Its name comes from the colossal statue of an earlier emperor that stood nearby. Three quarters of the building still stands today.
events.revealBlurb: 80 CE — inaugurated by Emperor Titus, son of Vespasian who had started construction eight years earlier. The colossal statue in question was of Nero, which Vespasian had rededicated as the sun god. Most of the travertine facing was stripped in medieval times for Renaissance building projects.

events.title: Angkor Wat Completed
events.blurb: A Khmer king completed a vast temple complex in his capital, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and later converted to Buddhist use. Covering over 160 hectares, surrounded by a moat, topped with a central tower 65 metres high, and decorated with 1.6 kilometres of bas-relief carvings illustrating Hindu epics, it was the largest religious monument in the world. After the Khmer capital shifted in the 15th century, the jungle gradually overgrew the complex, which was rediscovered by European travellers in the 19th century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1150 — King Suryavarman II, in the capital of the Khmer Empire (modern Cambodia). It appears on the Cambodian flag — the only national flag featuring a building. French explorer Henri Mouhot's 1861 account brought it to Western attention, though it had never actually been "lost."

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Panama Canal Opens
events.blurb: A 77-kilometre canal cutting across the narrowest part of the Central American isthmus opened to international shipping, after a US-run construction effort that had finished a French attempt abandoned two decades earlier amid malaria, yellow fever, and bankruptcy. The canal used a system of locks to raise ships 26 metres above sea level across the continental divide. It cut the sea route from New York to San Francisco by over 12,000 kilometres.
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1914 — the ship SS Ancon made the first full transit. The American construction was made possible partly by controlling yellow fever and malaria through mosquito eradication. The 1977 Torrijos-Carter treaties returned the canal to Panamanian sovereignty in 1999.

events.title: Hammurabi Stele Carved
events.blurb: A Babylonian king had 282 laws carved onto a 2.25-metre-tall pillar of black basalt, topped with a relief showing him receiving his authority from the seated sun god Shamash. The laws range from compensation for surgical malpractice to rules on bride prices, with the refrain "if… then" throughout. The stele was carried off as war booty to Susa 600 years later and discovered there in 1901.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1754 BCE — Hammurabi, 6th king of the First Babylonian Dynasty. "An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth" comes from here — law 196. Now in the Louvre. A second copy with slight variations was later found and is in Istanbul.

events.title: Van Gogh Paints The Starry Night
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Dutch painter, voluntarily committed to a mental asylum in a Provençal town, painted from memory — and through the bars of his east-facing window — a night sky filled with swirling nebulae and stars dozens of times their actual size, above a village with an exaggeratedly prominent church steeple. He considered the painting a failure. It is now among the most recognized images in Western art.
events.revealBlurb: June 1889 — Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum, Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. The village in the picture does not match the actual view. The Museum of Modern Art in New York has owned it since 1941. Recent research suggests the sky's swirls resemble actual fluid turbulence.

events.title: Mona Lisa Stolen
events.blurb: An Italian handyman who had worked at a Paris museum hid overnight in a storage closet, walked out the next morning in his worker's smock carrying a 77 by 53 cm wooden panel under his arm, and disappeared for two years and four months. The panel was a portrait by Leonardo da Vinci of a Florentine merchant's wife. The theft made worldwide news; Picasso and the poet Apollinaire were briefly questioned as suspects. The picture had been little known until this moment.
events.revealBlurb: August 21, 1911 — Vincenzo Peruggia. He was caught in Florence 28 months later trying to sell it to the Uffizi. He served seven months in Italian prison and was celebrated as a patriot by many Italians. The theft made the Mona Lisa internationally famous.

events.title: Dalí's Persistence of Memory
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Spanish surrealist painted a small oil on canvas — only 24 by 33 cm — showing four pocket watches, one covered in ants, draped limply over a tree branch, a bier, and a distorted horse-headed figure in a landscape of Catalan coast. He said the idea came from contemplating a runny camembert cheese. The ants, the soft watches, and the empty landscape have become visual shorthand for dreamlike unreality.
events.revealBlurb: 1931 — Salvador Dalí. Now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Dalí painted a second version, "The Disintegration of the Persistence of Memory," 23 years later. He is said to have visualized in reverse: imagining the picture whole and then painting what he saw.

events.title: Kahlo's The Two Fridas
events.blurb: A 32-year-old Mexican painter produced her largest painting — two life-sized self-portraits seated side-by-side on a bench, their hearts exposed and linked by an artery, against a stormy sky. The double figure depicted her divided heritage (her Mexican and European sides) and also the raw aftermath of her divorce from a fellow painter, which had become final three months earlier. She would remarry him a year later.
events.revealBlurb: 1939 — Frida Kahlo, shortly after divorcing Diego Rivera. Now in Mexico City's Museo de Arte Moderno. It was the largest canvas she ever painted, about 1.7 metres square. Kahlo's work reached superstar popularity only decades after her 1954 death.

events.title: Battle of Bunker Hill
events.blurb: American militia who had occupied two hills on a peninsula north of Boston overnight were assaulted by British regulars advancing uphill in three waves. The defenders — reportedly told "don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" to conserve ammunition — inflicted heavy casualties on the first two waves before running out of powder and being driven from the ground. The British held the field but lost over 1,000 men; the American cause gained enormous moral prestige.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1775 — fought mostly on Breed's Hill; misnamed after the adjacent Bunker Hill. British commander: General Thomas Gage. American commander killed in the retreat: General Joseph Warren. Within days, Congress appointed George Washington commander-in-chief.

events.title: Louis XVI Executed
events.blurb: A former French king, convicted by the National Convention of treason for allegedly conspiring with foreign powers against the revolution, was beheaded by a relatively new device on a Paris square as drums drowned out the opening lines of the speech he attempted to deliver from the scaffold. His wife, an Austrian-born former queen, would meet the same end nine months later. The regicide radicalized the revolution's enemies and internal fears alike.
events.revealBlurb: January 21, 1793 — Louis XVI at the Place de la Révolution (now Place de la Concorde). The National Convention had voted 361-360 for death, a margin of one. His final words were cut off by drums: "People, I die innocent..." Marie Antoinette was executed October 16, 1793.

events.title: Napoleon Invades Russia
events.blurb: A French emperor crossed the Neman River into Russian territory with the largest army Europe had ever seen — 680,000 men drawn from across his continental empire. His objectives were to compel Russia back into a trade embargo against Britain and to break Russian military power. The Russians fell back, burning as they withdrew, refusing pitched battle. The French reached Moscow in September to find it empty and soon burning. The retreat home through a catastrophic winter would destroy almost the entire army.
events.revealBlurb: June 24, 1812 — the Neman crossing. Of the 680,000 who crossed east, perhaps 40,000 returned. The retreat featured the famous crossing of the Berezina River, where improvised pontoon bridges collapsed under packed refugees; tens of thousands died in the icy water.

events.title: Battle of Waterloo
events.blurb: A French emperor's army of 73,000 men, attempting to defeat the main Anglo-Allied and Prussian armies separately before they could unite, fought the Anglo-Allied force on a Belgian ridge for most of a muddy Sunday. The Prussian army arrived in the late afternoon on the emperor's right flank; by nightfall the French line had collapsed. The emperor fled; he surrendered to the British at a port three weeks later and was exiled to a rocky island in the South Atlantic.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1815 — Napoleon Bonaparte vs. the Duke of Wellington and Gebhard von Blücher. Napoleon was exiled to Saint Helena and died there May 5, 1821. "Meet your Waterloo" — a decisive and final defeat — entered English as a phrase.

events.title: Brazilian Independence
events.blurb: The son of the king of Portugal, who had been designated regent of the Portuguese colony of Brazil since his father returned to Europe, was handed a set of demands from the Portuguese parliament ordering him home to end what it saw as a de facto autonomous Brazilian government. Reading the letter on horseback by a small river near São Paulo, he drew his sword and shouted "Independência ou Morte!" — independence or death. He was crowned emperor of Brazil three months later.
events.revealBlurb: September 7, 1822 — Pedro I, beside the Ipiranga River. He would reign until 1831, when he abdicated to return to Portugal. His son Pedro II ruled Brazil for 58 years before a bloodless coup in 1889 created the modern republic.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Battleship Potemkin Released
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet director released a 75-minute silent film dramatizing a 1905 mutiny on a Russian imperial battleship. Its centerpiece, a massacre sequence on a flight of stone stairs in the Black Sea port city of Odessa, introduced a style of rapid associative editing that reshaped 20th-century cinema. A baby's pram bounces downward through the gunfire in a shot that has been quoted by dozens of later filmmakers.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 1925 — Sergei Eisenstein. The Odessa Steps massacre is fictional; no such event occurred in 1905. The pram shot has been homaged in The Untouchables, Brazil, and The Simpsons. Joseph Goebbels reportedly called the film "a marvelous film without equal."

events.title: The Jazz Singer Released
events.blurb: A Warner Brothers feature film about a cantor's son who runs away to become a vaudeville singer premiered at a Times Square theatre as the first full-length motion picture with synchronized recorded dialogue. The star, in blackface for most of the film, delivered the industry's first-ever spoken movie line: "Wait a minute, wait a minute. You ain't heard nothin' yet!" Within three years almost every Hollywood film was a talkie.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1927 — Al Jolson at the Warners' Theatre, NYC. The film's sound system, Vitaphone, used synchronized phonograph records rather than optical audio. The silent era ended astonishingly fast; by 1930 the major Hollywood studios had written off the previous decade's technology.

events.title: Psycho Released
events.blurb: A British-American director released a black-and-white thriller for a third of his usual budget, using his television crew, that broke every Hollywood rule: its marketed star was killed in the shower 45 minutes in, the real story shifted to a different protagonist, and theatrical exhibitors were barred from letting latecomers enter. The 45-second shower sequence, involving 77 camera setups in a week of filming, became the most analyzed passage in thriller cinema.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1960 — Alfred Hitchcock, starring Janet Leigh and Anthony Perkins. Hitchcock personally bought up copies of the Robert Bloch novel to limit spoilers. The shower-stabbing sound was a knife thrust into a casaba melon.

events.title: Jaws Released
events.blurb: A 28-year-old director released a 124-minute thriller about a great white shark terrorizing a New England beach resort. Principal photography, supposed to last 55 days, ran 159; the mechanical shark broke down constantly and was rarely shown, producing the film's signature off-screen menace. Released across a record number of screens nationwide with a saturation TV ad campaign, it invented the summer blockbuster.
events.revealBlurb: June 20, 1975 — Steven Spielberg. The shark's malfunctions forced Spielberg to rely on John Williams' two-note score to telegraph the threat. The film caused a measurable drop in US beach attendance for years afterward.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Ratified
events.blurb: New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the proposed Constitution, providing the three-fourths supermajority required to bring the new framework of government into effect and replace the faltering Articles of Confederation. The document created a federal republic with three separated branches of power — a design that had no exact precedent in world history.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1788 — New Hampshire. Rhode Island didn't ratify until May 1790 — over a year after the government had already begun operating. North Carolina waited until November 1789, after the First Congress had already convened.

events.title: Haymarket Bombing, Chicago
events.blurb: At a labor rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square called to protest the police killing of striking workers the previous day, an unknown person threw a dynamite bomb into a column of police officers, killing seven officers and at least four civilians in the ensuing explosion and gunfire. The incident became the defining trauma of American labor radicalism and led to the hanging of four men for conspiracy, despite the bomber's identity never being established.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1886 — Haymarket Square, Chicago. Nobody has ever been identified as the bomber. Governor John Altgeld pardoned the surviving defendants in 1893, calling the trial a miscarriage of justice — and was destroyed politically for it. The date May 4 became International Workers' Day in much of the world as a result of the Haymarket executions.

events.title: Nixon Resigns the Presidency
events.blurb: That evening, Richard Nixon became the first and only U.S. president to resign from office, delivering a nationally televised address from the Oval Office in which he announced his departure would take effect at noon the following day. The resignation came after the release of the "smoking gun" tape proved Nixon had personally directed the Watergate cover-up six days after the break-in, making his impeachment and Senate conviction certain.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 1974 — The Oval Office. Nixon's approval rating the week of his resignation was 24%. Gerald Ford pardoned him one month later, saying "our long national nightmare is over" — a pardon that likely cost Ford the 1976 election. Nixon is the only president ever to resign.

events.title: Lehman Brothers Collapses: 2008 Financial Crisis
events.blurb: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy — the largest bankruptcy in American history, with over $600 billion in assets — triggering a global financial panic that erased more than $10 trillion in U.S. household wealth and produced the worst economic downturn since the 1930s. The failure stemmed from the firm's enormous exposure to mortgage-backed securities tied to a collapsing housing market.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 2008 — New York City. The Federal Reserve and Treasury had just rescued Bear Stearns and Fannie Mae but declined to backstop Lehman. The Dow dropped 504 points that day — and lost another 33% over the next three months. TARP, a $700 billion bank rescue program, was signed into law 19 days later.

events.title: Obergefell v. Hodges: Same-Sex Marriage Nationwide
events.blurb: The Supreme Court held 5–4 that the Constitution guarantees same-sex couples the right to marry, requiring all 50 states to issue marriage licenses and recognize same-sex unions performed elsewhere. Justice Anthony Kennedy's majority opinion grounded the right in both the Due Process and Equal Protection clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 2015 — Washington, D.C. The case's lead plaintiff, Jim Obergefell, had sought only to have his name listed on his deceased husband's death certificate as the surviving spouse. When the ruling was announced, the White House was illuminated in rainbow colors that night.

events.title: Fall of France
events.blurb: German armoured divisions crossed a forested highland deemed impassable by military doctrine, bypassed the most elaborate fixed defences in Europe, and in six weeks forced the capitulation of a nation whose army was considered the strongest on the continent. An armistice was signed in the same railway carriage used for the previous war's peace.
events.revealBlurb: May 10 – June 22, 1940. The armistice was signed at Compiègne in Hitler's deliberate reversal of the 1918 Armistice humiliation — he had the original railway carriage brought out of a museum. France lost 92,000 killed in six weeks. A junior general named de Gaulle flew to London and refused to accept the result.
