events.title: Operation Barbarossa
events.blurb: Three million soldiers, 600,000 motorised vehicles, 3,600 tanks, and 2,700 aircraft crossed a 2,900-kilometre border in the pre-dawn darkness, launching the largest land invasion in military history. The defender's air force lost over a thousand planes in the first day, many of them still on the ground.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 1941. Stalin reportedly refused to believe his own border commanders' early reports and assumed the attacks were unauthorised provocations. The operation's codename referenced the medieval Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. By December, Germany had advanced 1,000 km but failed to knock the Soviet Union out of the war.

events.title: Italy's Armistice Announcement
events.blurb: A radio broadcast by a head of government announced that his country had signed an armistice with the opposing alliance, pulling out of an axis it had helped found, leaving its former partner's forces — which had already occupied key positions across the country — to decide how to respond. German forces immediately disarmed Italian troops and occupied cities across the peninsula.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1943 — Marshal Badoglio's broadcast at 7:42 PM. The armistice had actually been signed on September 3 but was kept secret. German Operation Achse activated within hours, disarming and capturing roughly 650,000 Italian soldiers. Many were sent to German labour camps; some 50,000 died in captivity. The king and Badoglio fled Rome before dawn.

events.title: Rosie the Riveter Campaign
events.blurb: A deliberate government and industry campaign to recruit women into heavy industrial and weapons manufacturing work portrayed a bandana-wearing figure flexing her arm above the slogan "We Can Do It!" alongside magazine illustrations that reached millions of households, reshaping public expectations of gender and labour across a nation at industrial-scale mobilisation.
events.revealBlurb: 1942–1943. The number of women in the US workforce rose from 12 million to 20 million — a 57% increase — by 1944. Women built B-29s, welded Liberty ships, and operated cranes. The Westinghouse "We Can Do It!" poster was seen by almost no one during the war; it was rediscovered in the 1980s and became an icon of the feminist movement.

events.title: Death of Franklin Roosevelt
events.blurb: A president who had led his country through twelve years of depression and global conflict collapsed while sitting for a portrait at a cottage in the hills, dying two hours later before anyone could reach him, leaving a vice president who had been kept so far from the centre of power that he did not even know his government had been secretly building an atomic bomb.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1945 — FDR died at 3:35 PM at the Little White House in Warm Springs, Georgia. Harry Truman was presiding over the Senate when a note summoned him to the White House. His first question to Eleanor Roosevelt was whether he could do anything for her; she replied: "Is there anything we can do for you? For you are the one in trouble now."

events.title: Pong Released in Arcades
events.blurb: A black-and-white rectangle containing two paddles and a bouncing dot was installed in a Sunnyvale, California tavern as a hardware test. The test machine broke within days — not from malfunction, but because the coin slot had overflowed with quarters. Atari scrambled to ship units nationwide, and the commercial video game industry was born.
events.revealBlurb: November 29, 1972 — Atari Inc., founded that June by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, shipped Pong to arcades. The Andy Capp's Tavern prototype jammed after a week because it held too many coins.

events.title: Pac-Man Debuts in Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: A yellow circle eating dots and fleeing ghosts through a maze seemed like a peculiar bet in an era dominated by shoot-'em-ups. It became the highest-grossing arcade game ever made, the first video game character to achieve mass-market celebrity, and the template for an entirely new genre. Its creator wanted a game that women would actually want to play.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1980 — Namco's Puck-Man (renamed Pac-Man for Western markets to prevent vandalism) went on location test in Shibuya, Tokyo. By 1982 an estimated 30 billion quarters had been inserted into Pac-Man machines worldwide.

events.title: North American Video Game Crash
events.blurb: The home video game market had grown so fast that no one noticed it had filled up with garbage. Retailers were buried in unsold cartridges, consumers had lost all trust, and by 1985 an industry that had been worth $3.2 billion two years earlier had collapsed to $100 million — a 97 percent decline. Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.
events.revealBlurb: 1983–1985 — Annual revenue fell from $3.2 billion (1983) to approximately $100 million (1985). The Atari landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico — long an urban legend — was excavated in April 2014 and confirmed to contain millions of E.T. cartridges.

events.title: Sonic the Hedgehog Released for Sega Genesis
events.blurb: Sega needed a mascot to fight Mario. The result was a blue hedgehog who could run faster than the screen could scroll, built around a physics engine that turned speed itself into the core gameplay mechanic. It shipped bundled with the Genesis in North America, helped Sega capture 65 percent of the console market.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1991 — Sonic the Hedgehog launched in North America for the Sega Genesis. Sega's North American market share climbed from 15% to 65% during the game's first year. The Sonic franchise has since sold over 1.5 billion games.

events.title: League of Legends Launches
events.blurb: A free-to-play adaptation of a Warcraft III fan modification launched quietly and grew into the most-played PC game on Earth. At its peak over 100 million accounts had been registered, and its annual World Championship filled football stadiums and drew broadcast audiences that dwarfed traditional sporting events. It invented a new genre name — MOBA — and made esports a career path.
events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Berlin Airlift Begins
events.blurb: When Soviet forces blockaded all land and water routes into the western sectors of a divided city, Western powers responded with the largest humanitarian airlift in history. At peak, a transport plane landed every 30 seconds, carrying 8,000 tons of coal, flour, and medicine a day to 2.5 million stranded residents.
events.revealBlurb: June 24, 1948 — the blockade began; the airlift launched two days later and ran 15 months. Pilots dropped candy bars on tiny parachutes for watching children; one became known as the "Candy Bomber." 101 people died during the operation.

events.title: Korean War Begins
events.blurb: In the pre-dawn darkness, roughly 75,000 soldiers of a northern peninsular state poured south across the 38th parallel, overwhelming border defenses and driving south within days. The United Nations Security Council, with the Soviet representative boycotting, voted to intervene — the first shooting war between major powers since 1945.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1950 — Kim Il-sung's forces crossed the parallel. The USSR was boycotting the UN over China's representation, which is why the Soviet veto didn't stop intervention. MacArthur's Inchon landing three months later turned the war.

events.title: Gulf of Tonkin Incident
events.blurb: A U.S. Navy destroyer reported it had been attacked by small torpedo boats off the North Vietnamese coast. Two nights later, the same destroyer and a second reported a second attack in bad weather — an attack that likely never happened. Within days, Congress passed a resolution authorizing the president to use "all necessary measures" in Southeast Asia, opening the door to full-scale war.
events.revealBlurb: August 2 and 4, 1964 — the second "attack" was almost certainly radar ghosts and jumpy sonar operators. The resolution passed the House 416-0 and the Senate 88-2. Declassified NSA documents in 2005 confirmed the fabrication.

events.title: August Coup Against Gorbachev
events.blurb: A committee of Soviet hardliners — the KGB chief, the defense minister, the vice president — placed the reform-minded Soviet leader under house arrest at his Black Sea dacha and announced on state television that he was "unwell." Three days of confusion followed. A reformist Russian president climbed atop a tank outside his parliament and defied the plotters. The coup collapsed in 60 hours, and so, effectively, did the union.
events.revealBlurb: August 19-21, 1991 — the tank-top defier was Boris Yeltsin. Gorbachev returned to Moscow to find his authority gutted; Yeltsin had eclipsed him. Within four months the USSR itself would be gone.

events.title: Soviet Union Dissolves
events.blurb: In a televised resignation speech, the last leader of a superpower announced the end of his office and, by implication, the end of the 69-year-old multinational state he had led for six and a half years. The hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered above the Kremlin for the final time and replaced with the Russian tricolor. Fifteen newly independent countries inherited the ruins.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1991 — Mikhail Gorbachev's resignation. The USSR formally ceased to exist the next day. Gorbachev lived another 31 years, mostly ignored at home and celebrated abroad, occasionally appearing in Pizza Hut and Louis Vuitton ads.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: Paradise Lost Published
events.blurb: A blind 58-year-old English poet, dictating to a rotating cast of scribes, completed a 10-book (later 12-book) epic poem retelling the Biblical account of the fall of man from the perspective of a sympathetically characterized Satan. Having narrowly escaped execution for his political writings under the restored monarchy, he was paid ten pounds for the manuscript. It would become the template for English epic poetry.
events.revealBlurb: 1667 — John Milton. He had gone blind in 1652 from untreated glaucoma. His daughters had to be taught to read — including Hebrew, Greek, and Latin — just so they could transcribe his dictations. "The mind is its own place..." is from Book I.

events.title: Leaves of Grass Published
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Brooklyn printer, essayist, and newspaper editor self-published a small quarto of 12 unrhymed, unmetered poems celebrating the American body politic in a language saturated with sexual frankness. It drew praise from Ralph Waldo Emerson and denunciation from almost everyone else. The author kept expanding and revising the volume for the rest of his life; the final 1892 "deathbed edition" contained over 400 poems.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1855 — Walt Whitman, self-published because no publisher would take it. He set much of it himself at a Brooklyn print shop. His job at the Department of the Interior was terminated in 1865 after the Secretary read a copy and called it obscene.

events.title: Anne Frank's Diary Published
events.blurb: Two years after the liberation of Nazi concentration camps and the death of his teenage daughter in one of them, a Dutch businessman published, after several rejections, an edited version of the diary she had kept during the two years her family had spent hiding in a secret annex behind his Amsterdam office. The book was a modest Dutch bestseller; translated into over 70 languages, it became the most widely read personal account of the Holocaust.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1947 — Otto Frank published "Het Achterhuis" ("The Secret Annex"). Anne had died of typhus in Bergen-Belsen in February 1945, two months before liberation. The diary has sold over 30 million copies.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: Intel 4004 Released
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley chipmaker released the first commercial microprocessor — a single integrated circuit 3 millimetres long containing 2,300 transistors, clocking at 740 kilohertz, capable of computing roughly as fast as the 30-tonne ENIAC 25 years earlier. It had been developed as a calculator chip for a Japanese customer. Its designers convinced Intel's management to retain the design rights and market it as a general-purpose product.
events.revealBlurb: November 15, 1971 — Intel 4004. Designers Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima. The 4-bit chip cost $200. Intel's 1971 product-line predecessor was the 3101 memory chip; it now sells trillions of transistors per year.

events.title: Sony Walkman Released
events.blurb: A Japanese electronics company released a portable personal cassette player, weighing 390 grams, with headphones instead of a speaker. It had no record function — unusual for a cassette player — and its CEO personally insisted on this as a way of encouraging private, solitary music consumption. The device created an entirely new product category and pulled portable listening out of the car radio and boombox and into the individual's pocket for the next quarter-century.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 1979 — Sony TPS-L2. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had wanted something compact to enjoy opera on long flights. The original name in Japan was "Walkman"; in the US, "Soundabout"; in the UK, "Stowaway." "Walkman" eventually won out globally.

events.title: Macintosh Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched a new desktop computer during a Super Bowl advertising spot, and formally introduced it at a shareholders meeting two days later. The machine had a 9-inch black-and-white screen, a mouse, a graphical user interface with icons and windows, and pull-down menus — none of which had previously shipped on a mass-market computer. It cost $2,495 and would struggle commercially against the cheaper IBM PC for years.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1984 — Apple Macintosh. Ridley Scott's "1984" Super Bowl ad ran on January 22. The original Mac shipped with 128KB of memory; Bill Gates had quietly promised Steve Jobs a version of MS Word for it.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Tesla Model S Released
events.blurb: A California electric-vehicle startup, founded a decade earlier and funded partly by the same entrepreneur who had sold PayPal, delivered the first units of a four-door luxury sedan with a fully electric drivetrain, over-the-air software updates, a 17-inch touchscreen, and a 500-kilometre range. Legacy automakers had considered electric cars a niche; the Model S made them convincingly better than gasoline vehicles in several important dimensions.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 2012 — Tesla Model S, led by Elon Musk. Motor Trend named it Car of the Year. The "Ludicrous Mode" software option made it accelerate 0-60 mph in under 3 seconds. Tesla passed $1 trillion valuation in 2021, briefly the first automaker to do so.

events.title: Snow's Cholera Pump
events.blurb: A London physician, investigating a cholera outbreak in a Soho neighbourhood that had killed 127 people in three days, mapped the cases and traced their common origin to a public water pump on Broad Street. He persuaded the local parish authorities to remove the pump's handle. New cases stopped almost immediately. His investigation established that cholera was a water-borne disease — against the reigning theory that it spread through "miasmas" in the air.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1854 — John Snow, Soho, London. His sketched map of the cases clustered around the pump is a founding document of epidemiology. The pump's water source had been contaminated by a nearby cesspit. A replica pump stands at the site today, with its handle symbolically removed.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine Used on a Human
events.blurb: A French chemist administered the first human dose of an experimental rabies treatment to a nine-year-old boy who had been severely bitten by a rabid dog two days earlier and faced certain death without intervention. The boy survived, and the successful case launched the practice of post-exposure vaccination for infectious disease.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: First Human Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon transplanted the heart of a 25-year-old accident victim into a 53-year-old grocer in a nine-hour operation at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town. The recipient survived 18 days before dying of pneumonia; the same surgical team performed a second transplant 13 days later — that patient lived 19 months.

events.title: CRISPR-Cas9 Published
events.blurb: A team of molecular biologists led by a pair of American and French scientists published a paper in Science describing how a bacterial antiviral system — clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and an enzyme — could be programmed in the laboratory to cut DNA at any desired sequence. The tool made gene editing orders of magnitude cheaper and faster than previous methods. A patent fight between two universities consumed much of the ensuing decade.
events.revealBlurb: June 28, 2012 — Jennifer Doudna (UC Berkeley), Emmanuelle Charpentier (Umeå). They shared the 2020 Nobel in Chemistry. Feng Zhang at the Broad Institute applied CRISPR to mammalian cells separately; the patent dispute over commercial rights has yet to be fully resolved.

events.title: Tulsa Race Massacre
events.blurb: An armed white mob, deputized by local police and in some cases flown in biplanes to drop makeshift bombs, attacked an affluent Black neighborhood in an Oklahoma oil city nicknamed "Black Wall Street." Over 18 hours they burned 35 blocks of homes and businesses, killed an estimated 100 to 300 residents, and arrested 6,000 survivors. Nobody was ever prosecuted.
events.revealBlurb: May 31 to June 1, 1921 — Greenwood District, Tulsa. The massacre was scrubbed from local newspapers and school curricula for 75 years. A state commission finally investigated in 2001. Mass graves are still being exhumed.

events.title: Rosa Parks Arrested
events.blurb: A 42-year-old department-store seamstress and longtime NAACP secretary refused to give up her seat on a city bus in an Alabama capital when the white section filled up and the driver demanded the first row of Black seating. She was arrested for violating municipal segregation ordinances. The local Black community organized a one-day bus boycott that became a 381-day boycott.
events.revealBlurb: December 1, 1955 — Montgomery, Alabama. Parks was not, as legend has it, "too tired" to move — she was a trained activist who had attended a civil rights training school months earlier. Her act was calculated. A 26-year-old new preacher in town, Martin Luther King Jr., was chosen to lead the boycott.

events.title: Greensboro Sit-Ins
events.blurb: Four Black college freshmen sat down at the segregated lunch counter of a downtown variety store in a North Carolina city and politely ordered coffee. When refused service, they stayed seated until closing. They returned the next day with more students. Within two months, similar sit-ins had spread to 55 cities in 13 states, and the variety-store chain desegregated its counters.
events.revealBlurb: February 1, 1960 — Woolworth's lunch counter, Greensboro. The original four were students at North Carolina A&T State University: Ezell Blair, Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil, David Richmond. Part of the counter is now in the Smithsonian.

events.title: Civil Rights Act of 1964 Signed
events.blurb: President Lyndon Johnson signed the most sweeping civil rights legislation since Reconstruction, outlawing discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in employment and public accommodations — ending the legal architecture of Jim Crow segregation. The bill passed after the longest Senate filibuster in history: 57 days.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1964 — The White House. Johnson reportedly told an aide after signing the bill, "We have lost the South for a generation" — a reference to the political realignment he expected. Johnson signed the bill with 75 ceremonial pens, handing them to civil rights leaders and the bill's sponsors.

events.title: Stonewall Riots
events.blurb: A routine police raid on a Mafia-owned gay bar in a Greenwich Village of Manhattan turned into a six-night uprising when patrons — many of them drag queens, street kids, and trans people of color — fought back rather than submit to arrest. The confrontation catalyzed the modern LGBTQ rights movement; the first Pride marches were held on its first anniversary.
events.revealBlurb: June 28, 1969 — Stonewall Inn, NYC. Pivotal figures included Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera. The riot ignited the Gay Liberation Front, which modeled itself on the Black Panthers. June is now Pride Month across much of the world.

events.title: First Ancient Olympic Games
events.blurb: A religious festival held every four years in honour of Zeus at a sacred grove in the western Peloponnese began with a single footrace — a sprint of about 192 metres — won by a cook from the nearby city of Elis. Over subsequent centuries, the games expanded to include additional running events, wrestling, boxing, pankration, pentathlon, and chariot racing. The festival ran continuously for nearly 1,200 years before a Christian emperor banned it.
events.revealBlurb: 776 BCE — traditional date of first games at Olympia; winner Coroebus of Elis. The festival was abolished by Emperor Theodosius I in 393 CE as part of his suppression of pagan rites. It was revived as the modern Olympics in Athens, 1896.

events.title: Pelé Wins First World Cup
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Brazilian forward, playing in his first senior international tournament, scored two goals in the World Cup final as Brazil beat the host nation 5-2 to win football's greatest prize for the first time in the country's history. He became the youngest player ever to score in a World Cup final; his performance vaulted Brazilian football onto the world stage. He would go on to win two more World Cups over the following 12 years.
events.revealBlurb: June 29, 1958 — Pelé (Edson Arantes do Nascimento) at the Råsunda Stadium, Solna, Sweden. Brazil 5, Sweden 2. Pelé was carried off the field by his teammates at the end. He remains the only player to win three World Cups.

events.title: Maradona's Hand of God & Goal of the Century
events.blurb: An Argentine forward, playing a World Cup quarterfinal against England four years after a war over Atlantic islands the two countries had fought, scored two goals in four minutes. The first was a blatant handball that the referee missed; the player later described it as scored "a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God." The second, four minutes later, was a solo 60-metre dribble past five English players from the halfway line — widely considered the greatest goal in World Cup history.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 1986 — Diego Maradona at Estadio Azteca, Mexico City. Argentina 2, England 1. Argentina went on to win the tournament. Maradona later admitted the first goal was not only illegal but intended as a kind of revenge for the Falklands War. He died at 60 in 2020; Argentina went into three days of national mourning.

events.title: Tiger Woods Wins First Masters
events.blurb: A 21-year-old American golfer, playing in his first Masters as a professional, won the prestigious Augusta tournament by 12 strokes — the largest margin in the event's history — with a record-setting 18-under-par total. He was the youngest winner of a Masters, the first with African ancestry, and the first of Asian heritage. The club had admitted its first Black member only seven years earlier. Viewership had doubled the previous year's; his arrival reshaped the demographics, marketing, and money of professional golf.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1997 — Tiger Woods at Augusta National. He would win 15 major championships across a career including three more Masters wins. His dominance of the sport from 1997 through 2008 has been widely called one of the most influential individual runs in professional sports.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Johnstown Flood
events.blurb: After days of heavy rain, a poorly maintained earth dam built to create a private lake for a Pennsylvania hunting club gave way, releasing 20 million tons of water onto the steel-mill town 23 kilometres downstream. The wall of water reached speeds of 65 km/h and was 18 metres high. It killed 2,209 people in 10 minutes.
events.revealBlurb: May 31, 1889 — Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The hunting club's members (including Andrew Carnegie and Henry Clay Frick) were never successfully sued. The flood launched the American Red Cross onto the national stage; Clara Barton ran relief operations for five months.

events.title: San Francisco Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake ripped a 477-kilometre tear through the fault running up the California coast, hitting a West Coast boom city just after 5 AM. The shaking was severe, but the four-day fire that followed — fed by broken gas mains and fought with limited water from shattered pipes — did most of the damage, destroying 80 percent of the city and killing around 3,000.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1906 — San Francisco. The mayor authorized dynamiting buildings to create firebreaks; most of the dynamiting actually spread the fire. The opera singer Enrico Caruso, in town for a performance, vowed never to return. He didn't.

events.title: Tunguska Event
events.blurb: A massive explosion in the atmosphere above a remote Siberian forest flattened some 80 million trees over an area of 2,150 square kilometres. Eyewitnesses 60 kilometres away were thrown from their chairs. Seismic stations across Europe registered the blast. The first scientific expedition did not reach the site for 19 years. No impact crater was ever found.
events.revealBlurb: June 30, 1908 — Tunguska, Russian Empire. Current consensus: a stony asteroid 50-60 metres across exploded about 8 kilometres up. If it had arrived five hours later, it would have hit St. Petersburg. The date is now International Asteroid Day.

events.title: European Heat Wave
events.blurb: A prolonged period of extreme heat, with temperatures over 40°C across much of western Europe, killed an estimated 70,000 people, mostly elderly apartment-dwellers in cities poorly equipped for such conditions. France alone lost 15,000 lives. Morgues ran out of space; refrigerated trucks were requisitioned.
events.revealBlurb: August 2003 — France, Italy, Spain, UK, and Germany hit hardest. Paris reached 40°C. Many elderly victims were discovered by returning holidaymakers weeks later. France rewrote its social services to check on isolated seniors; subsequent heat waves in 2006, 2019, and 2022 killed far fewer.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.
